title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). The experiment used a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine). A single shared initial candidate was generated per task by gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120). A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applied intent-constraint and workflow-policy checks and triggered ≤1 repair only when validator.violation_count>0. Outcomes: baseline success = 120/120 (1.00); guarded success = 120/120 (1.00). Contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Validator traces show repair_applied=false for all guarded episodes. We incorporate peer-review clarifications (shared-generation semantics, repair-trigger logic, and artifact-grounded explanation of statistical degeneracy) and document execution accounting, per-topology results, representative validator traces, preregistration alignment, and reproducibility artifacts archived with the run.

sections.introduction:
Automating network-configuration tasks with generative LLMs promises operational speed and reduced manual effort, but syntactically plausible commands can violate workflow constraints (make-before-break, required shutdown→change→restore) and cause outages. Prior work therefore argues for tool-augmented pipelines (generate→validate→repair), digital twins, or veto layers that check generated candidates before enactment. Practical evaluation of such guardrails requires executable, closed-loop tests that reveal semantic failures beyond token-level correctness. We posed a tightly scoped, preregistered question: does inserting an executable emulator-based validator into a generate→validate→repair loop reduce semantic (network-level) failures of LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow?

To isolate validator and repair effects from generation variance we used a deterministic paired design with one shared initial generation per task (independent_condition_generation=false). This choice intentionally separates two mechanisms: (1) the LLM's ability to produce valid candidates and (2) the validator/repair subsystem's ability to detect and remediate invalid candidates. The paired design measures only the marginal effect of validation/repair on identical generated candidates. Our report gives the preregistered confirmatory analysis, execution accounting, per-topology breakdown, representative validator diagnostics, and an artifact-grounded discussion of why the run produced a ceiling/null outcome and what that implies for future evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Benchmarks and tool papers increasingly stress that command-level correctness underestimates operational failure risk. Recent emulator- and verifier-backed evaluations expose semantic errors that purely syntactic tests miss and motivate generate→validate→repair architectures (see representative works and surveys). Prior benchmarks demonstrate both frequent model failures on complex workflow constraints and measurable gains from integrating formal or executable validators; however, many published evaluations rely on synthetic or limited testbeds and vary in model/tool diversity.

Our experiment builds on this literature by preregistering a confirmatory paired test that isolates validator/repair efficacy given a fixed generation policy. Unlike multi-model leaderboards, our study intentionally holds generation constant to probe the incremental utility of an executable validator and a single-step repair policy. This positioning complements prior work that measures end-to-end agentic performance across heterogeneous model/tool stacks: where those studies assess combined system-level gains, our design asks whether the validator/repair stage can improve outcomes when the generator is held fixed and already produces a candidate.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and experimental plan: The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1. The design was paired-binary with exactly N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks; the preregistration specified three topology classes (edge, core, leaf–spine) with 40 tasks deterministically assigned to each class. Each paired observation used a single shared initial candidate generated by the declared hosted model (gpt-5-mini). The execution contract limited per-task generation to one initial call and allowed up to one repair call if the validator flagged violations.

Generation and model configuration: All candidate generation used gpt-5-mini under the archived model configuration (execution/model_configuration.json). The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 120 and maximum_model_calls_planned = 240; the observed model calls reflect one shared generation per pair (execution manifest fields: model_calls_used = 120, planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240).

Validator and repair policy: The deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, validator_version = 5.0) executed intent-constraint checks and workflow-policy validations (examples: make-before-break, required shutdown→change→restore; validator applied full_intent_constraint_validation scoring). Per the preregistration and archived implementation, a guarded repair was invoked only when validator.violation_count>0; archived validator traces show repair_applied=false for every guarded episode (execution/scoring/*.json). Repair budget: ≤1 repair iteration per guarded episode; because no violations occurred, repairs were never attempted.

Primary estimand and inference: The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (proportion reduction in emulator-observed semantic failures). The prespecified primary test was the exact two-sided McNemar with alpha=0.05. We computed a paired-difference estimate and a bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval using 10,000 resamples with seed=1729 (analysis artifacts record bootstrap_seed = 1729 and bootstrap_resamples = 10000).

Inclusion/exclusion and missingness rules: Technical/instrumentation failures (emulator provisioning, harness crash) would be excluded and logged; none occurred. The analysis executed a complete-pair primary approach as preregistered. Contamination checks (duplicate outputs, cross-condition cache reuse) were recorded; none triggered exclusions (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty). Deterministic consistency checks (provider_call_audit, episode accounting) passed (deterministic_reconciliation.json).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and raw outcomes: The run completed planned_episode_count = 240 (120 pairs) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Analysis/condition_summary.csv shows baseline = 120 successes, 0 failures; guarded = 120 successes, 0 failures; success rates = 1.0 for both conditions. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) records n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0.

Per-topology breakdown: Tasks were deterministically assigned 40 per topology class as preregistered. For each topology the archived condition_summary shows:
- Edge (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
- Core (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
- Leaf–spine (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
These per-topology counts are reflected in execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries and in the archived scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-0000XX-*.json).

Confirmatory statistics and degeneracy: With no discordant pairs (n_10 = n_01 = 0) the exact McNemar two-sided p-value equals 1.0 and the paired-difference estimate equals 0.00. The preregistered bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (seed=1729) is [0.00, 0.00]; the analysis log records these bootstrap parameters (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). The zero-width CI and p=1.0 reflect statistical degeneracy due to a ceiling effect (both conditions achieved 100% success); they do not provide evidence of equivalence nor confirm that guarded repairs are unnecessary in broader settings. We added a concise artifact-grounded explanation: the bootstrap CI is degenerate because each resample of paired binary outcomes draws from an empirical contingency with zero discordant pairs, producing identical resampled paired differences and therefore a single-value percentile interval.

Repair diagnostics and representative validator traces: For every guarded episode archived validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and validator_trace.repair_applied = false. Representative scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json, task-000002-guarded.json, task-000003-guarded.json) show normalized_response matching normalized_reference and violation_count = 0. The run therefore produced no repair activity, rendering preregistered secondary metrics about repair frequency vacuous.

Missingness, contamination, and accounting checks: analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 and zero technical failures. Contamination summary is empty (analysis/contamination_summary.csv). Deterministic reconciliation and provider-call audit entries are consistent (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json and execution manifest fields). All archived artifact hashes are recorded in the execution manifest.
sections.discussion:
Why the ceiling/null outcome occurred: The run's shared-generation design intentionally removed generation variance; the single shared candidate per task was already emulator-valid for the curated task bank and frozen prompting strategy. Because repairs were conditional on validator-detected violations and none were observed, the guarded pipeline performed identically to baseline for this paired design. This design choice therefore limited the experiment's ability to demonstrate repair effectiveness on independently generated invalid outputs. The result documents that, for this fixed generator and this synthetic task bank, the validator found no semantic violations; it does not generalize to settings where generators produce invalid candidates or where validators expose additional failure classes.

Practical implications: The artifact-backed ceiling result should not be read as evidence that guarded pipelines are unnecessary in practice. The deterministic harness used a specific model (gpt-5-mini), a frozen prompt/policy, and a synthetic, curated task distribution (intent constraints and workflow policies encoded in the task manifest). In diverse production settings—different models, prompt perturbations, multi-vendor devices, partial observability, adversarial inputs—validators and repairs will likely detect and remediate failures.

Design lessons for future experiments: To measure repair effectiveness under realistic generation variance, future confirmatory tests should adopt independent per-condition generation (allow the guard to see different LLM outputs than baseline) so that repairs can be credited for correcting generator errors. Additional design variants include increasing repair budget (multiple repair iterations), testing multiple models and prompt perturbations (the preregistration included exploratory prompt-perturbation plans), and expanding validator fidelity (multi-vendor behavioral models or production-rooted incident corpora). Our archived manifests explicitly support these follow-ups: the task_manifest records difficulty strata (medium/hard/very_hard) and required_sequence metadata that can be used to stratify future analyses.

Threats to validity: Internal validity — the shared-generation pairing isolates validator/repair effects but introduces a sensitivity limitation: it can mask repair gains that would appear only when baseline generation fails. Construct validity — the deterministic emulator validator operationalizes semantic correctness via encoded workflow policies; while reproducible, it simplifies vendor heterogeneity and runtime telemetry available in production. External validity — tasks were synthetic and deterministic and therefore may underrepresent noisy or adversarial production incidents; only one model was tested. Conclusion validity — the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) were violated by the observed ceiling, rendering the primary test uninformative for the intended effect size. All of these points are documented in the archived preregistration and execution manifests.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, producing n_11=120 (baseline and guarded successes) and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed=1729). The result is narrowly scoped: it documents a ceiling effect on this curated synthetic task bank and a shared-generation design that prevented the guarded pipeline from exercising repair behavior. We incorporated reviewer-requested clarifications (per-topology counts, repair-trigger policy, and artifact-grounded explanation of the degenerate bootstrap CI). Future work should relax shared-generation constraints, widen model/prompt diversity, expand repair budgets, and evaluate guardrails against more production-rooted incident corpora to meaningfully measure repair utility in realistic NetOps deployments.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
